diagnosis.what_is_wrong: A short, CPU-bound `ttworker` burst consumed nearly all four CPUs and caused severe runnable-task delays, plausibly explaining why the coding task took longer. The kernel evidence ties the impact to scheduler starvation during the burst, rather than disk, network, or memory pressure.
diagnosis.evidence: Compared the burst with adjacent pre-period 02:47:26.200–02:47:31.100 and post-period 02:47:35.400–02:47:37.400. `sched_stat_runtime` attributes about 15.33 CPU-seconds to `ttworker` during the burst, averaging 3.87 cores over 4.1 seconds on the four CPUs visible in raw scheduler records; the surrounding process total was about 0.36 cores before and 0.07 cores after. In `run_python` wakeup-to-next-switch matching, `claude` had 15 matched burst wakeups with median delay 1,560 ms, p90 2,446 ms, max 2,696 ms, versus pre/post medians of 0.018/0.016 ms; `mi-scavenger` was also delayed. The process lifetime and raw scheduler/exit records place the worker run from about 02:47:31.2 to 02:47:35.3. Block, network, and writeback counts did not rise in the burst, and no reclaim/OOM family was found. A falsifying check would be no coincident rise in worker CPU and runnable delays; the workers ran this check and found the opposite. Wake/switch matches are incomplete (19/46 burst wakeups unmatched), so the measured delay distribution may omit some waits.
diagnosis.window_evidence: The worker appears in indexed activity at 02:47:31.200 and its CPU use rises sharply from that onset, reaching roughly 3.99 CPU-seconds per second through most of the run. Raw sched_process_exit records show its threads exiting from 02:47:34.782 through 02:47:35.382, and aggregate CPU/scheduling activity falls immediately afterward; adjacent pre/post wakeup delays return to millisecond-scale values. The window therefore covers the observed worker burst and its exit, with the post comparison beginning at 02:47:35.400.
